newsitem.title: USA: Hamas chief loses bid to stop U.S. extradition.
newsitem.headline: Hamas chief loses bid to stop U.S. extradition.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, U.S. Law Correspondent
A federal judge on Wednesday refused to stop the extradition of a Hamas political leader who is to be returned to Israel on charges of murder and other violent acts.

Mousa Mohammed Abu Marzook had asked U.S. District Judge Kimba Wood to determine if he was being wrongfully imprisoned through a procedure known as a writ of habeas corpus. Marzook argued that another judge had erred in ordering his extradition.
But Wood upheld U.S. District Judge Kevin Duffy's reasoning in issuing the extradition order.

"I hold that the evidence he relied upon is more than sufficient to sustain his ruling," Wood said. "The record supports the conclusion that the hearing accorded to Dr. Abu Marzook was eminently fair and impartial."
Abu Marzook's extradition will not be immediate because he can appeal the ruling. His lawyer could not be reached for comment.
In addition, the U.S. Secretary of State has not yet certified the deportation order.

In a May 7, 1996, ruling Duffy said he found that Marzook was involved in an "agreement to accomplish an unlawful act" -- the element needed to hold him responsible for violence carried out by the militant Islamic group.
The judge said that under federal law, Israel did not have to show that Abu Marzook committed the violence himself or even knew of the specific events.

"There is more than sufficient evidence to show that Abu Marzook was a member of the conspiracy known as Hamas and that the acts charged against him were foreseeable consequences of the conspiracy," Duffy wrote.
He said evidence showed that Abu Marzook "knew that Hamas members were committing acts of terrorism against civilians in furtherance of the goals of Hamas."

Last year Israel announced it had formally asked the United States to hand over Abu Marzook, alleging he was responsible as the head of Hamas's political arm for attacks that killed scores of Israelis.

Israel did not contend that Abu Marzook personally committed any of the violent acts but did charge that he is criminally liable because of his high-level role in allegedly directing, controlling and financially supporting Hamas's activities.

Abu Marzook was arrested on July 25, 1995, at a New York airport as he flew to the United States -- where he had lived for many years -- after immigration officials found his name on its "watch list" of people with "known or suspected ties to terrorist activities."

Israel had requested his arrest and his extradition, alleging that the U.S.-educated Gazan was involved in a number of fatal bombings, shootings and stabbings between 1990 and 1994 and has raised money for and controlled the leadership of the military wing of Hamas.
Abu Marzook has a home and business in Virginia but U.S. and Israeli authorities charge he frequently travelled to the Middle East to promote violence and undermine peace efforts.

In April Duffy ruled that Abu Marzook could not call Palestinian President Yasser Arafat or other high-profile witnesses to support his case against extradition. Cohen sought to introduce the testimony to support Abu Marzook's claim that he had been involved only in political matters, which are not extraditable charges.
